points.title: System implementation (changeover)
points.must: The stage in which the new system is installed and put into use, replacing the old system: install hardware and software, convert data, train staff, change over.

points.title: Implementation method
points.must: The plan for how the old system is replaced by the new one; the four methods are direct, parallel, pilot and phased.

points.title: Why implementation is risky
points.must: The system meets real data, real users and real workload for the first time, while the organisation cannot stop working; the method decides whether data is lost or work stops if the new system fails.

points.title: Data conversion and training
points.must: Data conversion = moving existing records into the format of the new system and checking them (typing paper records with verification, or export → transform → import, then comparing record counts / totals); training and documentation are needed with every method and must fit it.

points.title: Timeline of the four methods
points.must: A diagram or description showing old and new systems over time for direct (switch in one day), parallel (overlap), pilot (one site first) and phased (one module at a time).

points.title: Direct changeover
points.must: Old system stopped completely and new system started immediately on a fixed date; advantages: fastest, cheapest, one system; disadvantages: most risky, no backup, all staff trained before, whole organisation affected.

points.title: When direct is suitable
points.must: Small / simple / non-critical systems, the old system no longer works, or a new organisation with no old system (e.g. café ordering).

points.title: Parallel running
points.must: Old and new systems run at the same time with the same data and results compared; advantages: safest, old system as backup, results checked, gradual training; disadvantages: most expensive, double workload, slow.

points.title: When parallel is suitable
points.must: Critical systems where failure is unacceptable — bank, hospital, payroll, seaport ship tracking.

points.title: Pilot implementation
points.must: The whole new system is introduced in one part of the organisation (department, branch, class) first, then everywhere; advantages: only one site affected, errors fixed before rollout, pilot staff train others; disadvantages: slower, pilot site may not be typical, two systems in use.

points.title: Phased implementation
points.must: The system is introduced one module at a time across the whole organisation; advantages: only one part affected, gradual learning, cost spread; disadvantages: slowest, old and new parts must work together, careful planning.

points.title: Pilot vs phased
points.must: Pilot = whole system in one place first; phased = one part of the system everywhere at a time; with an example of each.

points.title: Comparison of the four methods
points.must: A table comparing direct, parallel, pilot and phased on speed, cost, risk, backup, staff workload and what each is best for.

points.title: Choosing a method and its factors
points.must: Factors: how critical the system is, structure of the organisation (similar sites / separate modules), budget and staff, time available, how similar old and new systems are, how well the system is tested; critical → parallel; similar sites → pilot; separate modules → phased; small, urgent or old system unusable → direct; justify with the scenario and mention the trade-off.

points.title: Scenario examples
points.must: At least three scenarios with the chosen method and a reason linked to the scenario (e.g. seaport → parallel, school club system for one grade → pilot, café → direct, hospital modules → phased).
